newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila reaches accord with U.S. on garments row.
newsitem.headline: Manila reaches accord with U.S. on garments row.

text.p: The Philippines and the United States reached an accord in early March on a dispute in the rules of origin for textile exports to the United States, a Philippine trade official said on Tuesday.
Philip Panlilio, deputy executive director of the Garment and Textile Export Board (GTEB), said the agreement was signed on March 5 and would be retroactive for one year beginning January 1, 1997.
Flexibilities in the accord should provide an estimated compensation of $60 million for the garment exports that had been affected by the U.S. ruling, he said.
Concurrently, the Philippines agreed to withdraw its unfair trade practice suit filed in 1996 with the World Trade Organisation, he said.
In July 1996, the U.S. imposed a rule under which garment exports would be credited to the country of origin.
Most of Manila's garment exports comprise textiles from Hong Kong and China on which the final processing or finishing touches were done in the Philippines.
The rule meant that Philippine sales were considered Chinese exports and ran the risk of being barred once China's export quotas were completed.
The Philippines had earlier estimated the new rule would cut export revenues by $30 million a year and affect 5,000 workers.
"Under this agreement, they (the U.S.) provided flexibilities," Panlilio said, wherein exporters may be able to tap unused quotas of garment articles.
The U.S. also agreed to advance by one year the lifting of the quotas on cotton and man-made fibre infant wear and thus, give exporters free rein to tap this market, he said.

Garments are the country's second largest selling product abroad. Garment exports totalled $2.787 billion in 1996, down from $2.868 billion in 1995, with the United States the biggest buyer at $1.649 billion, according to the GTEB.
